newsitem.title: FRANCE: New French wheat futures still in the doldrums.
newsitem.headline: New French wheat futures still in the doldrums.

text.p: French futures exchange MATIF is having a hard time rallying interest in its new milling wheat contract almost three months after its launch.
MATIF officials and main floor members met last Friday to discuss ways to help boost flagging volumes, a broker with a leading floor firm said.

But exchange officials played down the significance of what they called a "routine working meeting". It focused mostly on marketing and training techniques and not on the product itself, launched on July 5.
"We discussed neither the product nor possible changes in its characteristics," one MATIF official told Reuters.
The meeting took place as rival Amsterdam's Agricultural Futures exchange (ATA) is reviewing its own milling wheat contract launched last June.
ATA said earlier Wednesday it had no plans to close down its wheat futures despite very low interest.

MATIF wheat futures have attracted mostly foreign operators and large French trade groups but scant interest from powerful French grain cooperatives that fear U.S. style hedging techniques may threaten the EU's system of guaranteed prices and subsidies.
"Interest from French cooperatives is clearly lacking," one broker lamented.

Since July 5 the contract has traded a total of 3,293 lots over 60 sessions with a daily average of 55, MATIF statistics show. For the month of September, total volume was 1,224 lots. Daily volume fell to 58 lots last month from 153 on the day the contract was launched.
MATIF officials have carefully avoided setting an official target for success. But officials say privately they are looking for 1,000 lots of wheat a day in two years.
On the positive side, open positions, the sum of uncovered positions, have risen steadily to 680 lots by end-September.
Traders have blamed the low volumes seen in July and August on the timing of the launch in between harvests.
"Timing of the launch could not have been worse," one broker said, adding this explained the lack of interest shown for the now expired September contract.

MATIF officials link sluggish futures activity to low physical business during the summer months and expect business to pick up in autumn. They also see the contract as a key part of the exchange's long-term strategy to diversify beyond financial products.

When MATIF decided to launch wheat futures, world wheat prices were on a bull run as supplies were scarce and demand strong. But now prospects of bumper crops in most of the world and increased competition among suppliers is pressuring prices.

Brokers said MATIF may now have even harder time convincing reluctant farmers to use its hedging instruments when domestic prices are slipping towards intervention price levels guranteed by the European Union. --Paris newsroom +331 4221 5432
